title: "When the country depends entirely on partners, things tend to go wrong": global health and HIV/AIDS initiatives in Guinea-Bissau
From emergency relief to system strengthening: Stakeholder perspectives on official development assistance for reproductive, maternal, neonatal and child health in Guinea-Bissau
Perceptions of the usefulness of external support to immunization coverage in Guinea-Bissau: A Delphi analysis of the GAVI-alliance cash-based support
abstract: The aim of the present study was to understand the participation of global health initiatives (GHIs) in addressing the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Guinea-Bissau based on the insights of different social and political actors, representatives of GHIs, the Guinean government, and civil society organizations. A qualitative, descriptive, exploratory case study was conducted involving interviews with 36 participants. Thematic content analysis was employed. The discourses of the participants were organized into four main topics. The results indicate that, besides the government, at least 15 nongovernmental organizations and a strong partnership with Brazil were identified in the response to HIV/AIDS. The limitations and challenges of the government are related to the acquisition of funding and the management of the resources provided by GHIs. The contributions of GHIs were described as positive, considering the internal lack of funding and external dependence, with the Global Fund as the primary funder of HIV/AIDS response actions. This dependence interferes with the autonomy of management and affects coordination. The situation in Guinea-Bissau resembles that of several countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, in which the work of GHIs is characterized by a paradox: dependence on financial resources and the need to decolonize from external aid, which, to some extent, serves as a disciplinary device. Guinea-Bissau, a politically fragile West African nation, relies heavily on official development assistance (ODA) to sustain reproductive, maternal, neonatal and child health (RMNCH) services. This study explored how national and international stakeholders perceive the role, evolution and effectiveness of RMNCH-related ODA and how these perspectives compare with donor strategies. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 10 key informants and applied an AI-assisted, systematically validated framework to analyse 50 donor documents, integrating findings through comparative coding and convergenceâ€“divergence synthesis. Stakeholders viewed ODA as â€˜humanitarianâ€™ or â€˜emergencyâ€™ aid, substituting for the state rather than catalysing durable system change. Donor documents strongly emphasised coordination, alignment and ownership but tended to underplay political risk and institutional capacity limits. Triangulated analysis identified interlinked constraints: political instability and ministerial turnover, fragmented coordination despite multiple formal mechanisms, performative alignment with national plans, limited domestic financial contribution and an evolution toward vertical funding that risks further fragmentation. Findings point to the need for hybrid coordination arrangements combining national and international leadership, depoliticised and stable technical capacity within the Ministry of Public Health, longer and more flexible programme cycles with contingency mechanisms, and greater domestic financing and use of national strategic plans as a genuine framework for system strengthening. Introduction: Although many countries have improved vaccination coverage in recent years, some, including Guinea-Bissau, failed to meet expected targets. This paper tries to understand the main barriers to better vaccination coverage in the context of the GAVI-Alliance (The Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunisation) cash-based support provided to Guinea-Bissau. Methods: The analysis is based on a document analysis and a three round Delphi study with a final consensus meeting. Results: Consensus attributed about 25% of the failure to perform better to implementation problems; and about 10% to governance and also 10% to scarce resources. The qualitative analysis validates the importance of implementation issues and upgraded the relevance of the human resources crisis as an important drawback. The recommendations were balanced in their upstreamdownstream focus but were blind to health information issues and logistical difficulties. Conclusions: It is commendable that such a fragile state, with all sorts of barriers, manages to sustain a slow steady growth of its vaccination coverage. Not reaching the targets set reflects the inappropriateness of those targets rather than a lack of commitment of the health workforce. In the unstable context of countries such as Guinea-Bissau, the predictability of the funds from global health initiatives like the GAVI-Alliance seem to make all the difference in achieving small consistent health gains even in the presence of other major bottlenecks.
